newsitem.title: SPAIN: Madrid parliament rejects budget amendments.
newsitem.headline: Madrid parliament rejects budget amendments.

text.p: The Spanish parliament on Wednesday rejected opposition motions against an austere 1997 budget package which is crucial to Spain's hopes of joining a European single currency from the start.
The parliament voted by 176 votes to 161 against wholesale amendments put forward by the main opposition Socialists and the Communist-led United Left.

The draft budget is assured safe passage when the final vote is taken on November 22 on the combined votes of the ruling Popular Party and those of its allies in Catalonia, the Basque country and the Canary Islands.
"We are on the right path towards meeting the Maastricht treaty criteria," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said after Wednesday's vote.
Smaller regional parties took the platform on the second day of debate on the draft budget after the left-wing opposition parties presented their arguments on Tuesday.

The ruling conservatives' Catalan nationalist allies urged them to rigorously implement the 1997 budget, saying it was crucial to Spain meeting the criteria to join European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The biggest danger is not carrying out the budget. That would have an impact on interest rates," said Joaquim Molins, parliamentary speaker for the Catalan Convergence and Unity (CiU) coalition.
The moderate Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) pledged to back the package in exchange for regional tax concessions.
Although its five votes are technically superfluous, they would give the Popular Party (PP) a comfortable margin over the Socialists and the Communists in the final vote.
"It's proof of our capacity for dialogue, our capacity for agreement," said Aznar. "I am very satisifed that we have fulfilled a very important part of our political objectives and our programme."

The tax deal is based on measures the PP promised the PNV in return for backing Aznar's investiture in May. They include greater control over some types of revenues like special taxes on alcohol, tobacco and fossil fuels and non-residents' tax.
But unions criticised the vote, saying the budget placed the burden of adjustment on the poorest sectors of society.

"To balance the state's accounts, tilted in favour of the powerful, they are relying on those who have the least and on public sector workers," said Antonio Gutierrez, leader of the Workers' Commission union.

Aznar's ministers hope the austere budget package will allow them to meet stringent EMU criteria during 1997, the year on which would-be participants in the single currency will be tested for fitness.
The 1997 budget slashes total spending growth to just 1.7 percent by cutting or freezing outlays in all sectors except for pensions, health and regional transfers.
With inflation expected at 2.6 percent next year, it is the toughest budget since Spain's return to democracy in 1975.
Aznar took advantage of the vote to take an indirect swipe at his Socialist predecessor, Felipe Gonzalez, saying the debate had shown some groups' inability to provide an alternative.
Aznar and his aides on Tuesday blamed disarray in Socialist ranks for the main opposition party's decision to give the floor to two of its top economic men rather than to its leader.
Gonzalez, who ruled Spain for 13 years until May and was the architect of Spain's 1986 entry to the then European Community, has been an ardent supporter of EMU all along.
But the Socialists argue that if Spain manages to be among a first wave of EMU participants in 1999 based on this budget, it will be at the expense of employment and of social welfare.
